At the heart of this argument lies John Stuart Mill's harm principle, articulated in his seminal work On Liberty (1859): "The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others." 1) Individual autonomy / sexual liberty arguments

Claim: In liberal political theory, criminal law should not police private sexual behavior between adults unless it clearly harms others (the “harm principle”). Some proponents try to extend that logic to include certain human–animal interactions.

  • Privacy and bodily autonomy: The state should not criminalize intimate conduct occurring in private when it doesn’t produce demonstrable harm.

  • Resource allocation: Enforcement effort could be redirected toward clear animal-cruelty cases (neglect, violence, organized exploitation) rather than blanket prohibition.

2) Challenges in defining (and proving) “animal consent”

Claim: Consent is hard to define even in some human contexts; it becomes even harder with animals because they can’t give verbal, legally cognizable consent. Some decriminalization arguments try to treat this as a reason to avoid criminal law’s “all-or-nothing” approach.

Typical reasoning:

  • Consent-as-communication vs. consent-as-legal-capacity: Advocates sometimes argue that while animals lack legal consent capacity, they can show behavioral willingness (approach/avoidance, signs of stress, etc.).
  • Comparison to other animal contexts: People routinely interpret animals’ preferences and distress in:
    • training,
    • handling,
    • veterinary care,
    • husbandry. Proponents argue the law already relies on behavioral indicators of animal welfare, so “impossibility of verbal consent” should not automatically determine criminality.
  • Evidentiary concern: Because “consent” is not measurable in the same way as human consent, proponents argue that criminal law should focus on objective harms (injury, coercive restraint, distress indicators) rather than a categorical presumption.

Note: Critics respond that the inability to give informed, voluntary consent is not merely “hard to measure” but conceptually disqualifying—creating an inherent power imbalance and exploitation risk.

3) “No clear harm” in specific controlled circumstances (harm-based decriminalization)

Claim: Some argue that if an interaction is nonviolent, does not cause physical injury, does not involve coercion/restraint, and shows no signs of animal distress, then criminal law lacks a clear harm to justify punishment.

Typical reasoning:

  • Harm principle framing: Criminal prohibition should track demonstrable harm (injury, suffering, fear, long-term stress), not presumed harm from taboo.
  • Overbreadth concerns: Blanket bans can treat very different scenarios the same way (e.g., violent cruelty vs. ambiguous, non-injurious situations). Advocates argue for narrowing laws to target:
    • force or restraint,
    • injury,
    • exploitation (commercial or organized),
